title: Sidh Gosht close
hook: a conversation with other seekers, still worth having

segments.voice: Yesterday, dialogue, not debate: Nanak used the yogis' own words and never mocked them. Your line was answer kindly. Which question did you answer with salt instead of bite? Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

Most conversations vanish. Somebody says goodnight, the porch light goes off, and whatever was said lives on only in the two people who were there. A few get written down. Fewer still get sung. The talk between Guru Nanak and the Siddhs on the mountain did not vanish. It sits in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raga Ramkali, and Sikhs still read it and sing it. A conversation between seekers who did not agree, kept as scripture. For the last two weeks we've been sitting in that circle. Today we stand up and look back at it. Sidh Gosht close.
screen: `MOST CONVERSATIONS VANISH.` → `THIS ONE BECAME SCRIPTURE.` → `LOOKING BACK AT THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Walk around the circle once. It began with a question as old as strangers: who are you, where do you come from. Asked how to live, Nanak gave the lotus and the duck: in the water, not soaked by it. Asked why he left home, he said: to seek the Gurmukhs, the people turned toward the Guru. The yogis' earrings became the Guru's Word. Asked where it all began, he spoke of wonder. Asked where the mind lives, he said the Word steadies it. Then the answer some readers call the center of the whole dialogue: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. The world as an ocean, the Word as the boat. A guide is needed. The breath carries the Name. The true yogi is spotless in the middle of the soot. And, read beside a verse from the Asa di Var, the side that bows is the heavier one. That's a lot of ground. But notice what held it together. Not agreement. The yogis never stopped being yogis, as far as the text tells us. What held it together was that both sides kept talking. Questions were real questions. Answers were real answers, in the other side's own language. That may be the quietest teaching of the Sidh Gosht: a conversation with other seekers is worth having, and worth having all the way through. Sikhs keep this conversation in scripture, beside the Gurus' hymns of praise. That placement says something. Talking honestly with people who walk a different path can be part of the path itself.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU? THE DUCK STAYS DRY.` · `THE WORD IS THE GURU.` · `NOT AGREEMENT: THEY KEPT TALKING.` · `CONVERSATION AS PART OF THE PATH.` · then, large: `KEEP TALKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare for one deep conversation. Sit, and think of someone you'd like to really talk with: a friend who sees things differently, a parent, a neighbor whose faith isn't yours, a colleague you only ever discuss work with. Choose one real question you could ask them, the kind the yogis asked: where do you come from, what steadies you, what do you think it's all for. Hold the question. Then imagine listening to the whole answer without planning your reply. If you pray, you can ask for an open ear. If you don't, simply hold the person in mind. The bell holds the time.
Sidh Gosht close. The end of the dialogue with the yogis: two paths that didn't agree, a conversation that held, and scripture that kept it. Today's word.
Your line: keep talking. Today, ask that one real question, and stay for the whole answer. If it can't happen today, send the message that sets a time. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: The Sidh Gosht is in Raga Ramkali in the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikhs read it in the course of a full reading of the scripture, and kirtan singers sing stanzas from it.
